notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: You can greet, introduce yourself, and ask how someone is. Time to leave gracefully. The final, plainest parting is adiós — and, like the English goodbye, it's a tiny prayer worn smooth.
diphthong-io — the -iós is one glide, ee-OHS: ah-DYOHS, stress on the end (that's what the accent on ó marks — remember the acute-accent lesson).

adiós is a + Dios — "to God." It's the front half of an old blessing, a Dios te encomiendo, "I commend you to God" — said to someone setting off, when a journey was dangerous and you left them in God's keeping.
Every Romance sister kept the same farewell-prayer:

utterances: language: Spanish. goodbye: adiós. literally: "to God".
language: French. goodbye: adieu. literally: "to God" (à Dieu).
language: Italian. goodbye: addio. literally: "to God".
language: Portuguese. goodbye: adeus. literally: "to God".

segments.text: And English is doing the exact same thing without telling you: goodbye is a crushed-down "God be with ye." So adiós and goodbye are, at heart, the same sentence — a blessing for the road.
Dios ("God") from Latin Deus — the Deus of English deity, divine, adieu, and (via Greek Zeus, same root) the whole sky-god family.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: adiós is a final goodbye

segments.text: adiós leans toward a longer parting — you won't see them soon, or it's the end of the day. For "see you later / tomorrow," Spanish reaches for hasta …, which the rest of this chapter is about — and hasta has a surprising origin.

segments.instruction: adiós / adieu / addio / adeus — four "to God" farewells
segments.source: [YOU SAY: adiós / adieu / addio / adeus — four "to God" farewells]

segments.instruction: English "goodbye" = "God be with ye" — the same prayer
segments.source: [YOU SAY: English "goodbye" = "God be with ye" — the same prayer]

segments.text: What two words hide inside adiós? (a + Dios — "to God.") What English goodbye is built the same way? (Goodbye from "God be with ye.") Is adiós for a quick "see you soon"? (No — it's the longer/final parting; hasta … comes next.) Next: hasta, and a word Spain borrowed from Arabic.

Spanish says "see you later" as hasta luego — literally "until later." So the key word is hasta, "until." And hasta carries the single most important fact about Spanish's history: for nearly 800 years, much of Spain spoke Arabic.
silent-h — Spanish h is always silent: hasta = AHS-tah (no breath on the h at all). Stress the front.

hasta comes from Arabic ḥattā, “until, up to.” From 711 CE, Muslim armies ruled much of the Iberian Peninsula — al-Andalus — and Arabic was the language of government, science, and poetry there for centuries, until.
Spanish absorbed roughly four thousand Arabic words in that time — more of its vocabulary than from any source except Latin itself.
Most of those loans are nouns, and you can spot a huge number by the frozen Arabic article al- ("the") fused onto the front:
almohada (pillow), alcázar (fortress), alcalde (mayor), alfombra (rug), aduana (customs), álgebra, alcohol.
azúcar (sugar), aceite (oil), naranja (orange).

But hasta is rare and special: it is a function word — a preposition, part of the grammatical skeleton. Languages borrow nouns easily and grammar words almost never — so an Arabic preposition surviving in everyday Spanish shows how deep, how intimate, those centuries of contact were. (Its Latin rival ad "to"/usque "up to" simply lost.) You say a piece of al-Andalus every time you say goodbye.

segments.instruction: "hasta" then Arabic ḥattā — the same word, 1,300 years apart
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "hasta" then Arabic *ḥattā* — the same word, 1,300 years apart]

segments.text: What language is hasta from, and what does it mean? (Arabic ḥattā — "until.") Why is it remarkable that Spanish borrowed it? (It's a function word / preposition — languages almost never borrow those; it shows how deep the Arabic centuries went.) How do you spot many Arabic nouns in Spanish? (The frozen al- article: almohada, azúcar, álgebra.)

lessons.title: hasta aquí / hasta la noche — point to the limit
lessons.gloss: hasta points to an endpoint in space or time

segments.text: You know hasta means “until” or “up to.” Give that small word one spatial endpoint and one temporal endpoint, using only one new word.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: endpoints in space and time

segments.text: Aquí means here. Put it after hasta:
hasta aquí — up to here.
For a time endpoint, reuse la noche, “the night,” from Chapter 2:
hasta la noche — until the night / until tonight.
The same preposition points to a place or the end of a stretch of time. The next lessons will place new time words after it one at a time.
What does hasta point to? (An endpoint.) Give one spatial and one temporal example. (Hasta aquí; hasta la noche.) What is the only new lexical item? (Aquí, “here.”)

lessons.title: hasta luego — the everyday "see you later"

segments.text: This is the goodbye you'll actually use most — friendly, casual, open-ended. hasta luego: "until later." You already own hasta ("until"); today you add luego ("later"), and it has a very Latin backstory.
diphthong-ue — luego = LWEH-goh: the ue is a w-glide, lweh-.
The whole phrase: AHS-tah LWEH-goh.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the phrase

segments.text: hasta luego = "until later" becomes "see you later."
hasta = "until" (last lesson — Arabic ḥattā).

luego = "later / then / soon," from Latin loco, "at the place / at that point." The idea slid from place becomes point in time becomes "then, next, soon." So its cousins in English are all about place: local, locus, location, locate, al-loc-ate. Spanish moved loco from where to when.
A nice contrast: hasta luego fuses an Arabic word and a Latin word in three syllables — the two great layers of Spanish, shaking hands as you leave.
hasta + a time word is Spanish's whole toolkit of soft goodbyes. You'll build the other two this chapter:

utterances: phrase: hasta luego. "until …": later. when: the default "see you".
phrase: hasta mañana. "until …": tomorrow. when: leaving for the day.
phrase: hasta pronto. "until …": soon. when: you expect to meet again shortly.

segments.instruction: "luego" then English "local, location" — the loco "place" family
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "luego" then English "local, location" — the *loco* "place" family]

segments.instruction: "¡Adiós! … no — ¡hasta luego!" — feel the difference: final vs. soon
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "¡Adiós! … no — ¡hasta luego!" — feel the difference: final vs. soon]

segments.text: What does hasta luego literally mean? ("Until later.") What did luego's Latin root loco first mean, and what English words keep it? (Place — local, location, locus.) Which two language layers meet in hasta luego? (Arabic hasta + Latin luego.) Next: hasta mañana.

lessons.title: hasta mañana — "see you tomorrow" (and the ñ returns)

segments.text: Leaving for the day? hasta mañana — "until tomorrow." It brings back a letter you studied in the writing lessons: the ñ. Here it is, living in a word you'll say every evening.
enye-ny — mañana = mah-NYAH-nah: the ñ is the squished ny of "canyon" (your ñ writing lesson — the tilde is a tiny second n, remember). Three soft ah's: ma-ÑA-na.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the phrase

segments.text: hasta mañana = "until tomorrow" becomes "see you tomorrow."
hasta = "until" (Arabic ḥattā).

mañana = "tomorrow" — and "morning." One word for both, from Latin (hōra) maneana, "the early hour" (from māne, "in the morning"). The logic: the next "early hour" you'll see is tomorrow morning becomes mañana came to mean both morning and tomorrow.

The ñ, in the wild. Recall the writing lesson: ñ is a frozen nn — a scribe's shorthand for a doubled n. mañana comes from Latin maneana, whose n+ea palatalized (softened) into that single ñ sound. So the tilde is a little historical fossil sitting in the middle of "tomorrow."

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: same word, two meanings — context decides

segments.text: mañana means "morning" or "tomorrow"; the sentence tells you which. Paired with hasta, it's always tomorrow: hasta mañana, "until tomorrow."

segments.instruction: “mañana” once as “morning,” then once as “tomorrow” — context decides
segments.source: [YOU SAY: “mañana” once as “morning,” then once as “tomorrow” — context decides]

segments.text: What two meanings does mañana carry? (Morning; tomorrow.) With hasta, which one? (Tomorrow.) What sound is the ñ, and what is its tilde, historically? (The ny of "canyon"; a frozen doubled-n.) Next: hasta pronto.
The last of the "hasta …" trio: hasta pronto, "until soon" — for when you genuinely expect to meet again shortly. One new word, pronto, and it's hiding in plain sight in English.
hasta pronto = AHS-tah PRON-toh — a clean pr, a pure o.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the phrase

segments.text: hasta pronto = "until soon" becomes "see you soon."
hasta = "until" (Arabic ḥattā).
pronto = "soon / quickly / ready," from Latin promptus, "brought forth, ready at hand" (from prōmere, "to bring out"). Something prompt is brought out without delay — so pronto slid to "soon."

You already know its English twin: prompt (on time; to bring out a response), plus prompter, promptly, and the computer prompt (the cursor "ready" for input). Italian borrowed pronto too — it's what Italians say when they pick up the phone ("Pronto!" = "Ready!").
You now have Spanish's three soft goodbyes, sharpest to vaguest in time:

utterances: phrase: hasta pronto. until…: soon. nuance: you'll meet again shortly.
phrase: hasta luego. until…: later. nuance: the neutral default "see you".
phrase: hasta mañana. until…: tomorrow. nuance: you're parting for the day.

segments.text: …and adiós for the long or final goodbye.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "pronto" then English "prompt, promptly" — one family]

segments.instruction: the trio — hasta pronto / hasta luego / hasta mañana
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the trio — hasta pronto / hasta luego / hasta mañana]

segments.text: What does hasta pronto mean, and pronto's English twin? ("Until soon"; prompt.) What Latin word is it from, and its literal sense? (promptus, "brought forth / ready.") Order the three hasta goodbyes by time. (pronto becomes luego becomes mañana.) Next: put the whole farewell set together.

lessons.title: Practice — saying goodbye
lessons.gloss: closing a conversation — the full set of farewells

segments.text: No new words. This chapter's farewells — adiós and the three hasta … goodbyes — now close a real conversation, and fold back into the whole arc you've built since hola.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: choosing the right goodbye

segments.text: The choice is about when you'll meet again:

utterances: you're…: parting for good / a long time. say: Adiós.
you're…: expecting to meet again shortly. say: Hasta pronto.
you're…: just "see you" (neutral default). say: Hasta luego.
you're…: leaving for the day. say: Hasta mañana.

segments.text: Everything from Chapters 1–5, in one conversation:
— ¡Hola! Buenos días. Me llamo Ana. ¿Cómo se llama usted? — Me llamo Luis. Mucho gusto. — ¿Cómo está usted? — Bien, gracias. ¿Y usted? — Bien. Hasta mañana, Luis. — Hasta mañana, Ana. ¡Adiós!
adiós — the plain/final goodbye ("to God"; twin of goodbye).
hasta — "until," Spain's everyday Arabic word ( from ḥattā).
hasta luego / mañana / pronto — see you later / tomorrow / soon, each an Arabic + Latin handshake.

segments.text: Run the whole exchange, hola to adiós, without stopping.

Which goodbye for someone you won't see for a long time? (Adiós.) Which everyday word for "until" did Spanish take from Arabic? (hasta.) You can now open and close a conversation in Spanish. Next chapter: por favor and gracias' partner courtesies, then into everyday verbs.
